title: The Whole Earth Shaken
overview: Isaiah pictures a judgment that empties the earth because people broke their bond with God, ending with the LORD reigning in glory from Jerusalem.

parts.label: No one is spared (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: The LORD will empty and ruin the earth, and rank, money or religious office will protect no one. The Hebrew word here can mean either "the earth" or "the land," so scholars still debate whether Isaiah means the whole world or Judah in particular.

parts.label: A broken agreement (vv. 4-6)
parts.note: The reason given is that people broke God's laws and the "everlasting covenant," a lasting agreement; many think this means the promise God made with Noah for all humanity, though some read it as Israel's own covenant. Wrongdoing is pictured as polluting the ground itself, so the land withers and only a few people survive.

parts.label: The celebrations stop (vv. 7-13)
parts.note: Wine, drums and harps fall silent, and a ruined city sits with its gate smashed and its houses shut; the city is not named, and scholars are unsure which one, if any, is meant. The few survivors are like the last olives left after a tree is beaten, or the stray grapes left after harvest.

parts.label: Songs far off, grief close by (vv. 14-16)
parts.note: Survivors in distant lands to the west and east sing praise to the LORD, and their song gives glory to "the righteous"; the Hebrew could mean God as the Righteous One or righteous people, and translations differ. The prophet cannot join in, because he sees betrayal and treachery still going on around him.

parts.label: Nowhere to run (vv. 17-20)
parts.note: The image comes from hunting: noise drives animals into a pit, and any that climb out are caught in a trap, so whoever escapes one disaster falls into the next. The sky opening above recalls the start of Noah's flood, and the earth staggers like a drunk and collapses under the weight of its guilt.

parts.label: The LORD reigns (vv. 21-23)
parts.note: God punishes the kings of the earth and a heavenly army or host above, which may mean the stars people worshiped or spiritual powers thought to stand behind nations; the exact meaning is uncertain. Even the sun and moon look pale beside the glory of God ruling from Jerusalem in front of its elders.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether this chapter mainly describes judgments in Isaiah's own era, such as the fall of Judah or of surrounding nations, or a final judgment at the end of history.
think: When a disaster strikes rich and poor, powerful and powerless alike, what does that show about the things people usually count on to keep them safe?
